metadata.title: The Names Nothing Checks
metadata.persona: Synthetic Kokoro af_bella voice reading Weiting Wang's own words (disclosed in the opening beat, on the end card, and in SOURCES.md)
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: show-tell style: opens on the hesitant writer plus the terms card, no verdict card; Your Turn is the Claude.ai composer. The spoken outro stays, but names the author instead of the instructor: the INFO 7375 assignment requires narrating as oneself and forbids the instructor's name, persona or credit line, so the outro handle and narration are the author's. OUTRO-LOCK is expected to flag this; see FRICTIONAL.md.
metadata.audience: Unity gameplay programmers who write code with an AI assistant, and reviewers looking at tools and AI-engineering work
metadata.honesty_note: Nothing in this film exists yet except the Unity game referenced in B04 and B08. Every drawing of the proposed tool is labelled 'proposed' on screen. Past tense appears only in B04 and B08, both of which describe work actually done in spring 2026. CORRECTED 2026-10-13: an earlier cut claimed the console says nothing about a wrong animator parameter. Unity does warn about that one. The claim now names the shader property, which Unity's own documentation says has no effect and no message, and B02B states the difference out loud. See FACTCHECK.md rows 3 and 4.

beats.narration_text: Hi. These are Weiting Wang's words, read by a synthetic voice. I build games in Unity. When I asked an AI for gameplay code, I used to check whether it compiled. That turned out to be the wrong question.

show.event: types 'Can an AI write Unity code'
backspaces 'that compiles' -> 'that actually runs' on the spoken correction

props.text:
Can an AI write Unity code
that compiles

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the naive compile question and corrects it to the real one: whether it runs.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Three terms. A shader property: a name stored in a Unity asset, not in the code. A string reference: code reaching that name as quoted text. And a silent failure: wrong code that compiles, runs, and does nothing.

beats.narration_text: Code can only reach those names as text. A string. Material dot set float, open quote, glow active, close quote. That quoted word is the whole link.

beats.narration_text: An assistant that only reads your C sharp files cannot know the name inside the shader graph. So the name in its answer is a guess, and no gate here catches a guess.

beats.narration_text: What I will build does the opposite. It reads the assets and writes down every name that really exists.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it is false alarms. A string is not always written out in full. Flag good code, and nobody runs the tool twice.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Pick a project you know well and ask your AI assistant for code that uses a name stored outside the source files: an animator parameter, a shader property, a config key. Then open the file that actually defines that name and compare. Tell me whether the assistant read it or guessed it. Then check two things yourself. Did it say out loud that it was unsure? And would anything in your build have caught it if it was wrong?
